texte.1c9e1f9c8029: Your tool: three terms for every rook endgame
texte.24046f153b36: The Philidor position: a draw through activity
texte.691a10baec9d: The Lucena position: winning by building a bridge
texte.4629fd7052f1: The Vancura position: a draw against the rook's pawn
texte.22c55f122b1c: Cutting off, White to move. Gray arrow: the rook on e1 blocks the e-file; three files (d, e, f) lie between the king on g6 and the pawn on c5.
texte.8df7ff6ac5b5: Why is the rook on e1 so valuable for White here?
texte.0fae0928311a: It defends the pawn on c5 from behind.
texte.c999d715e8af: It keeps the black king on the far side of the e-file, far away from the pawn on c5.
texte.6b37206873ed: It threatens mate on the 8th rank.
texte.793ed423f30a: Cutting off means: the rook blocks a file between the king and the pawn. The more files lie in between, the better for the attacker; three are often enough.
texte.9ff0aac4aa83: Short and long side, White to move. The black king stands on the short side (g-file), the rook on a6 on the long side. Gray arrow: four files lie between the rook and the pawn; that is enough for its checks.
texte.a99ba3c46563: Why is the black rook well placed on a6?
texte.f07a13e1d3e2: It can capture the pawn on f5 right away.
texte.b14521fa257e: It protects its own king against a mate on the 8th rank.
texte.78ad618e298f: It has enough distance: if the white king walks toward it, the king abandons its pawn.
texte.cd190f5a9ed0: Four files lie between a6 and f5. From this distance, the rook can give check from the side without the king reaching it.
texte.9c03019b6db5: The Philidor position, White to move. Gray: the king on e8 stands in front of the pawn, the rook on h6 blocks the 6th rank. The white king cannot get to d6, e6 or f6.
texte.42469afecfc7: Why does 1. e6 change Black's plan?
texte.4ed6d47cea82: With the pawn on e6, the white king no longer finds a hiding place: the rook goes to the back and gives checks.
texte.36c487fa5cf1: Now Black can capture the pawn on e6 with the king right away.
texte.dbc946974e04: Black now has to trade rooks.
texte.f3d9b63b1c30: As long as the pawn stands on the 5th rank, the rook holds the 6th rank. After e6, the king can no longer hide from checks from behind.
texte.5ba267b87a9c: After {z1}, White to move. Gray arrow: the rook now gives check from behind, and the pawn on e6 takes away the white king's hiding place.
texte.7e2d07d98074: When Philidor no longer works: King to the short side
texte.d086846ac2f5: King on the short side, rook on the long side; Black to move. Gold arrow: only {z1} holds the draw.
texte.fc1a348a3197: The rook pins the pawn on e6.
texte.4a5e17450430: The check from the side starts a series; the white king cannot escape it without abandoning the pawn.
texte.9f2ca8ee300b: Black is preparing to trade rooks on a7.
texte.78e98ef58815: With three files of distance, the checking distance is enough. If the king walks toward the rook, the pawn on e6 is left behind on its own.
texte.43c47cd95002: With the rook on b8 instead of a8, after {z1}; White to move. Red arrow: the check. Gold arrow: {z2}.
texte.15e717abbc73: Why does White escape the checks with 3. Kd7?
texte.bab75d1ce394: Kd7 threatens mate on the 8th rank right away.
texte.34b9af3b5db9: The king attacks the black king.
texte.1f1b3e851cec: The rook on b8 is too close to the pawn: the king walks toward it, and the checks stop.
texte.88154a92db1b: After 3... Rb7+ 4. Kc6, the king attacks the rook. With the rook on a8, it would have been too far away for that.
texte.017691ddf642: After {z1}, Black to move. Red arrow: the king attacks the rook; the checks are over.
texte.59d99e8cd87b: Basic picture of the Lucena position, White to move. Red: the king on e8 stands in front of its pawn and cannot get out. Gray arrow: the rook on f1 cuts off the black king along the f-file.
texte.d952702f7cbb: Why does White start with 1. Rg1+?
texte.5c40ad806377: The rook wants to deliver mate on the g-file.
texte.facf53ebae90: White wants to trade the rook for the rook on a2.
texte.60a4e6e793c3: The check drives the black king one file farther away from the pawn.
texte.f2997339a5ec: On g7, the king could win the pawn back after a rook trade (Fig. 9.13). On h7, it is one step too far away for that.
texte.e18376f4edc6: Building the bridge move by move
texte.ca02d4296da3: After {z1}, Black to move. The black king has been driven away to the h-file. Gray arrow: from g4, the rook later reaches the bridge square e4.
texte.c1b54c01dfb4: After {z1}, White to move. Red arrow: the king has left e8 and gets checked.
texte.d30d914fef9f: After {z1}, White to move. Red arrow: the check. Gray arrow: the king goes to the pawn's file, to e5.
texte.c61bf4ac0f7e: Why does the king go to e5?
texte.f3fff7725206: From there it defends the square e4: on the next check, the rook on g4 steps in between.
texte.e2f50e8e25a2: It wants to attack the rook on d1.
texte.d7446c84431f: On e5, the pawn on e7 protects it against all checks.
texte.e6ef3a2b5b06: After 6... Re1+ comes 7. Re4: the bridge stands, and the king defends the rook. The promotion square e8 can no longer be held.
texte.bc0f9cbfa2e0: After {z1}, Black to move. Gray arrow: the bridge stands, the king defends the rook on e4. Red: the promotion square e8 can no longer be held.
texte.43cc999a2d7b: Why drive the king away first?
texte.4e5e7b27335d: Warning picture: the same bridge, but the black king is still on g7. Black to move. Red arrow: {z1} holds the draw.
texte.b4e37723adac: Why does 1... Rxe4+ hold the draw here?
texte.3606b840c4e6: After the trade, White is stalemated.
texte.816d4472fe0f: After 2. Kxe4, the king goes to f7 and captures the pawn on e7.
texte.bd918979e340: The rook on e4 was undefended.
texte.31e64948ff55: The bridge only helps if the defender's king is far enough away. That is why, in the Lucena position, White first drives it farther away with a check.
texte.38e1862b94d1: After {z1}, White to move. Red arrow: the pawn on e7 falls, draw.
texte.525ded27fc22: The Vancura position, Black to move. Red arrow: the rook on f6 attacks the pawn on a6 from the side. The white king defends the pawn, the rook on a8 wants to move away. Gray: the black king waits on g7.
texte.92657c5cb798: Why does Black give check with 1... Rf5+?
texte.1d119b9226c8: It wants to trade the rook for the pawn.
texte.df093a00e17c: It prepares a mate on the 5th rank.
texte.5e182a0f7b36: The king has to step aside and stay with the pawn; afterwards the rook attacks a6 from the side again.
texte.cc2b6c513ec4: Checks and sideways attacks on the pawn alternate. That way, White makes no progress.
texte.aea133bb25e9: White to move. The king on f7 guards neither h8 nor h7. Gold arrow: only {z1} wins.
texte.7538aa184fb9: The rook gives check and drives the king away.
texte.cb6e7d5c755a: It threatens a8=Q; if Black captures with 1... Rxa7, 2. Rh7+ wins the rook with a skewer.
texte.a91744636a90: It protects its own back rank.
texte.219d94892627: The rook makes room for the pawn and lies in wait on the h-file. That is why, in the Vancura picture, the king stands on g7 or h7.
texte.a50b22d4ed3b: After {z1}, Black to move. Red arrow: the skewer. The king has to step aside, then the rook on a7 falls.
texte.44dad543d432: Cutting off, Black to move. Gray arrow: the rook on d1 blocks the d-file.
texte.6401b586ad69: White to move wins, for example with {z1} (gold arrow): the king takes the square d4 (gray) away from the black king.
texte.6a7bf425bcba: The king attacks the pawn on e4 directly.
texte.58e8db84d107: It defends the promotion square e1.
texte.1674e2f72c96: It takes the square d4 away from the black king and gets closer to the pawn.
texte.58ab3078ef0d: That is how White wins. If it were Black to move, 1... Kd4 would hold the draw, because the king blocks the white king's path (Fig. 9.20).
texte.6dad703dbacc: Black to move holds only with {z1} (gold arrow): the king blocks the white king's path. Draw.
texte.a7dea4620ef4: Black to move. After {z1}, {z2} mates. Gold arrow: only {z3} holds the draw.
texte.9db83b044466: Why does Black promote to a knight?
texte.12be811c020d: It gives check, and after 1... b1=Q??, 2. Re1 would have been mate.
texte.737ae2435e3b: In the endgame, a knight is stronger than a queen.
texte.ce613f0dd20a: The knight attacks the rook on e2.
texte.12f591e36962: Underpromotion: with check, Black gains the time it lacks against the mate. The result is a draw.
texte.b207237b47b8: Two connected passed pawns on the 6th rank, Black to move. Red: one of the two becomes a queen, whatever the rook tries.
texte.b98959594dfe: White to move. Red arrows: the rook on b7 attacks the pawns on a7 and f7 along the 7th rank. White wins the pawn back with Rxa7; afterwards Black has to keep defending the pawn on f7.
texte.13f601e4bde1: Four against three on the kingside, White to move. Red arrow: the black rook on a2 stands actively on the 2nd rank and attacks f2. Such positions are considered hard to win.
texte.b04549f324a1: Rooks behind passed pawns, White to move. Gold arrow: the rook on a1 stands behind the passed pawn on a5 and becomes more active with every pawn move. Gray: the black rook on a7 stands in front of it and is tied down.
texte.c32c459405b7: Why is the rook on a1 better placed than the rook on a7?
texte.f7e8cb49c61b: It stands closer to its own king.
texte.4a1cd60b183a: It stands behind the passed pawn: every pawn move gives it more room, while the rook on a7 only blocks.
texte.88965c8b3741: It protects the 1st rank against a back-rank mate.
texte.2b73e191d064: Rooks belong behind passed pawns. The rook in front of the pawn is tied to the blockade and becomes more passive with every pawn move.
texte.3dba8f5cd0d6: White to move. Gold arrow: the rook trade {z1}.
texte.180686d4599c: Why does White trade rooks with 1. Rxb8+?
texte.5a50da3b144f: The pawn endgame is won: the outside passed pawn on a4 ties down the black king.
texte.633c0985b210: White wants to get rid of a lost rook endgame and hold the draw.
texte.d197cbd9a7ce: After the trade, Black is mated at once.
texte.a0301cc756d5: The plan from the table: trade into the won pawn endgame. If the black king has to stop the a-pawn, the white king has a free path on the other wing.
texte.ab61c1bb576c: After {z1}, White to move. Gold arrow: the outside passed pawn on a4 ties down the black king; the pawn endgame is won.
texte.9de79cd2c481: White to move. The pawn on d2 is about to promote, the white king is far away. Gold arrow: {z1} starts the series of checks.
texte.79413955c702: What is the goal of the series of checks that starts with 1. Qe4+?
texte.b76df221e3a1: Perpetual check, because a draw is the most White can get.
texte.66fef92d96d9: To capture the pawn on d2 right away.
texte.0b707207db3c: To force the black king onto d1, in front of its pawn, so that the white king has time to come closer.
texte.503b10f22af3: When the king stands in front of the pawn, the pawn cannot promote. Every such pause brings the white king one step closer.
texte.9847888af0ec: After {z1}, White to move. Gold arrow: {z2} drives the king to d1, in front of its pawn.
texte.7b774ca63bf0: After {z1}, White to move. The king blocks its own pawn. Gold arrow: the white king uses the pause, {z2}.
texte.a68a23b0718e: Stalemate alert: bishop's pawn and rook's pawn
texte.1c05179f4b37: Bishop's pawn, White to move: draw. Red arrow: {z1} stalemates the king on a1.
texte.280057286441: White to move, the king on e3 is close enough. Red arrow: the natural capture {z1}. Gold arrow: the right way, {z2}.
texte.ebb893402f8c: Why does White play 1. Qf3+ instead of 1. Qxf2 right away?
texte.fe169cbc7bf9: The pawn on f2 is defended by a black piece.
texte.58022e4c9bf8: 1. Qxf2 would be stalemate; after 1. Qf3+ Kg1, the queen captures on f2 with check.
texte.4a28c403b57a: Stalemate alert with the bishop's pawn: only the in-between check brings the king out of the corner. Then the capture is no longer stalemate.
texte.3f3f027c05e6: After {z1} – stalemate. The king on h1 is not in check, but the queen controls g1, g2 and h2 (red).
texte.8730707a7809: Black to move. Red arrow: the queen trade {z1} loses. Gold arrow: only {z2} holds the draw.
texte.df24df0dc4d1: Why does Black give check with 1... Qd1+ instead of trading queens?
texte.3f5b3d1de674: A queen trade is not allowed as long as a pawn stands on the 7th rank.
texte.61cd5ed07404: After 1... Qxg2+ 2. Kxg2, the pawn on a7 promotes; with checks, on the other hand, Black holds the draw.
texte.9ad614c6bb6b: The defender calculates the checks first. After Qd1+ Qg1 Qf3+ Qg2, White never gets to promote.
texte.77a676aea910: Opposite-colored bishops, White to move: a draw despite the extra pawn. Gray: the king blockades on the dark square c7; the white bishop (arrow) can never attack it.
texte.93168c806366: Why does Black hold the draw here despite being a pawn down?
texte.a7dab72a8af9: The bishop on d6 can capture the pawn on c6 right away.
texte.bda1ce91c87e: White is to move and is in zugzwang.
texte.b2ca3825bd3a: The king on c7 blockades on a dark square that the light-squared bishop on f3 can never attack.
texte.fc15d57f6438: That is the fortress with opposite-colored bishops: a blockade on the color the opponent's bishop cannot reach.
texte.cffcf160c414: Two connected extra pawns, White to move: draw. Gray: king and bishop control d5 and e5, the squares in front of the pawns.
texte.2b88834cb6e4: Two separated extra pawns, White to move: won. Gold arrows: the passed pawns on both wings.
texte.892896dee4a2: Same-colored bishops: the passed pawn decides
texte.2a76e58a78ea: Same-colored bishops (both on light squares), White to move. Gold arrow: only {z1} wins. Gray arrow: the bishop on f3 controls the diagonal up to the promotion square a8.
texte.ccbafe57a26b: The pawn runs at once; the bishop on f3 controls b7 and a8, and the black king can no longer get in front of it.
texte.21dd0162e6a6: a6 blocks the diagonal of the bishop on d7.
texte.c48a79d5cda3: a6 prepares a king march to g5.
texte.23bbd37d62e7: With same-colored bishops, there is no safe blockade on the other color. Whoever brings their passed pawn forward quickly enough wins.
texte.c7a2e4880565: Black to move loses. Red: no knight move guards the promotion square h8.
texte.02f930a27030: Black to move holds the draw. Gold arrows: only {z1} or {z2} guards h8 in time.
texte.e0f98ecfaf8a: The wrong bishop, White to move. The bishop on c4 moves on light squares, the promotion square h8 (red) is dark. The black king cannot be driven away: draw.
texte.6150e7cb41e3: Why does White not win here despite the bishop and the extra pawn?
texte.9f396236b235: The pawn on h6 is pinned.
texte.6cd3a0db8ec4: The bishop on c4 never reaches the dark promotion square h8, and the king in the corner cannot be driven away.
texte.be9e55a2ff67: White is in zugzwang and has to give up the bishop.
texte.14a25e4205c1: With a rook's pawn, the bishop needs the color of the promotion square. Otherwise the defending king simply stays in the corner.
texte.6290a5093186: Bishop vs. knight with pawns on both wings, White to move. Gray arrow: the bishop on d3 works along the whole diagonal up to h7; the knight on d6 needs several moves for every switch of wings.
texte.9c5dc4927ba4: The right corner, White to move: draw. The bishop on g3 moves on dark squares, the corner a8 is light. Red arrow: the check {z1}. Gray arrow: {z2} blocks it.
texte.1fc5c91b16f5: The wrong corner, White to move. The corner h8 has the color of the bishop. Gold arrow: {z1} (only move) {z2}.
texte.7c024fd317a7: Why does 1. Rh4+ decide at once?
texte.7fe82856788f: The rook attacks the bishop on g7.
texte.bd484ea351c2: The king on h8 can escape to g8, and the bishop is lost.
texte.7d663fe41d66: Black has to interpose 1... Bh6, and 2. Rxh6 is mate.
texte.8fb722cb9ab3: In the wrong corner, the king has no way out. As the side with the bishop, the king belongs in the corner of the other color (Fig. 9.43).
texte.faa1d3413137: The black rook is already on the 1st rank. Should Black give check from behind right away?
texte.8ecfeb7e648f: No. After {z1}, the pawn on e5 shields the white king against checks from behind, and {z2} is threatened: the king then stands on a key square, and the pawn endgame is won. Correct is {z3}: the rook blocks the 6th rank, and the Philidor position stands. Other waiting moves also hold the draw, but only the barrier on the 6th rank makes the defense simple. Remember: first block the rank in front of the pawn. The rook only goes to the back once the pawn has advanced.
texte.d3f36170cc68: After 1... Rd1+? 2. Ke6!, the pawn on e5 shields the king against checks from behind, and White threatens the rook trade into the won pawn endgame. Correct is 1... Rh6!: the rook blocks the sixth rank, and only when the pawn advances does it go to the back.
texte.08b072ea8806: White threatens {z1}. How does Black defend, and where does Black's king belong?
texte.44b2ae8bd65d: The king belongs on g8, on the short side: {z1}. The rook on a1 stands on the long side and has enough checking distance there: {z2} is met, for example, by {z3}, and White makes no progress. After {z4}, on the other hand, the king stands on the long side and in its own rook's way: {z5}, and the f-pawn runs. The in-between check {z6} also holds the draw. Remember: king to the short side, rook to the long side.
texte.9028effbe6bc: The king belongs on g8, on the short side; the rook stays on the long side and has enough distance there for checks. After 1... Ke8? 2. Rb8+ Kd7 3. Kg7, the king stands on the long side in its rook's way, and the pawn runs.
texte.2e02189e71de: How does White win? Describe the rook's route and the king's route.
texte.dc3a28050785: {z1} brings the rook to the 4th rank. White does not need to drive away the king on g7, since three files already lie between it and the pawn. Then the white king leaves the promotion square and zigzags down the board, for example {z2}, and the bridge stands. Many other first moves also win, for example {z3}: the rook defends the pawn from behind, and the king walks toward the black rook. Remember: rook to the 4th rank, king out in a zigzag, rook in between.
texte.2e07863b51d3: 1. Re4 puts the rook on the fourth rank; the black king is already far enough away. Then the white king leaves the promotion square in a zigzag, and on the last check the rook steps in between with Rc4.
texte.ac5b90996a42: White has just played a6–a7. What does Black have to do now?
texte.e916ea64f602: The rook has to go to the a-file at once: {z1} It attacks the pawn, and the white rook can no longer leave a8. An in-between check ({z2} or {z3}) followed by the rook move to the a-file is just as good. The king stays on g7 or h7 throughout. Every other move loses, for example {z4}. Remember: when the rook's pawn stands on the 7th rank, the rook belongs behind it and the king on g7 or h7.
texte.f3c12c8b8224: 1... Ra6! attacks the pawn and ties the white rook to a8; the king stays on g7 or h7. Every other move loses, for example 1... Kh7? 2. Rb8 Ra6 3. a8=Q.
texte.dd91e8ae8b6e: Only one move wins. Find it.
texte.0e0faf33a691: {z1} The rook occupies the promotion rank, far enough away from the black king. Then the white king arrives in time, whatever Black plays: {z2}, and the pawn falls. {z3} or {z4} is also met by {z5}. Every other first move, on the other hand, lets the pawn escape. Remember: against a far-advanced pawn, the rook belongs on the promotion rank, far away from the opposing king.
texte.2aaa1b70196b: 1. Rb1! occupies the promotion rank far away from the black king, and the white king arrives in time via b2, c2 and d2. Every other first move lets the pawn escape.
texte.66351a41e253: Only one move wins. Find it and explain why.
texte.6b5dba3cf0e2: {z1} The rook blocks the 5th rank: the black king can only get in front of its pawn by the detour via b6 and a5, and that takes too long. After {z2}, the white king is there in time. If the pawn runs on its own, the rook picks it up as soon as it reaches the 3rd rank: {z3}. Before that, the rook must not leave the 5th rank: after {z4}, the king defends its pawn, and the position is a draw. Remember: cutting off also works along a rank.
texte.ba85b0f6ce35: 1. Rg5! blocks the fifth rank, and the black king can only get in front of its pawn by a detour; by then the white king has arrived. If the pawn runs on its own, the rook picks it up from behind or on b3.
texte.fcbc56c22430: Can the rook still stop the two pawns? Back up your answer with a move sequence.
texte.8adca983441b: Yes, since only one pawn has reached the 6th rank: {z1}, and both pawns fall, just as after {z2}. {z3} followed by {z4} also wins. Every other move loses, for example {z5}, and both pawns are too far advanced. Remember: the rook has to stop connected passed pawns before both reach the 6th rank.
texte.31aa579f0328: Only one pawn stands on the sixth rank, so the rook still holds: 1... Rb8! 2. c6 Rxb6 3. c7 Rc6, and both pawns fall. After 1... Rc8? 2. b7, both are too far advanced.
texte.8f5cbf9fda6e: What is White's fastest way to win?
texte.07fac56a3f2d: {z1} The king takes b2 and leaves the black king the square b1. After {z2}, {z3} mates. The obvious moves {z4} and {z5}, on the other hand, give stalemate, since the king on a1 then has no square and the pawn on a2 has no move. Remember: never take away the king's last square without giving check.
texte.d05be593aa87: 1. Kc3! takes b2 away from the king and leaves it b1, so that after 1... Kb1, 2. Qg1# is mate. The obvious moves 1. Kc2?? and 1. Qb4?? give stalemate.
texte.420839dac80a: Can White win? Explain your answer.
texte.fcfe2beed30b: No. The bishop on d4 moves on dark squares, the promotion square a8 is light: it is the wrong bishop. If the black king stays in the corner on a8, White cannot drive it away, and the game ends in a draw. Remember: with a rook's pawn, the color of the promotion square decides whether the bishop helps.
texte.ce256624e50d: The bishop moves on dark squares, the promotion square a8 is light. If the black king stays in the corner, White cannot drive it away: draw.
texte.e99d3c112ebb: Why the king belongs on g7 or h7
